citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, a final boxed answer, a difficulty level (1–5), and one of seven subject tags (Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, Precalculus). The dataset is designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models.
name: MATH
rai:annotatorDemographics: For human evaluation, six university students studying computer science participated. Four participants are authors on the paper. The other two are friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. Participants were offered remuneration but volunteered. All had one hour to complete 20 problems without a calculator.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems are curated from competition mathematics (AMC, AIME, etc.) and are carefully curated by the competition mathematics community. Each problem has a step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. Difficulty levels (1–5) are assigned following AoPS conventions. Answers follow strict formatting rules to enable automatic exact-match evaluation using the \boxed{} command delimiter.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States. Problems are tagged by difficulty (1–5) following AoPS conventions, and span seven subjects.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems and solutions are written in LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is notably challenging even for humans (a computer science PhD student attained ~40%, a three-time IMO gold medalist attained 90%). Models achieve only 3–6.9% accuracy, indicating the benchmark may be too hard for current models to show meaningful differentiation. Accuracy increases only very slowly with model size, suggesting that simply scaling Transformers will not solve MATH in the foreseeable future.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow strict formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent encodings (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and \dfrac{x}{y}) are treated as identical. Units may be included or omitted; spaces are ignored; common equivalent number representations (e.g., 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as the same.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that even 40% accuracy on MATH for a machine learning model would be impressive but would have ramifications for cheating on homework. They explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. Solving MATH with machine learning would be of profound practical and intellectual significance given the broad reach and applicability of mathematics.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; measuring and forecasting reasoning capabilities of large language models. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to be used to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not describe multiple independent annotations per item; each problem has one ground-truth solution from the competition source.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No annotation platform is used; problems are sourced directly from competition archives (aops.com). Human evaluation was too small (6 participants) to use a platform.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality analysis is described; answers come from official competition solutions.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The paper states competitions span decades but gives no specific collection timeframe or date range for when data was gathered.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the MATH dataset collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation of missing values is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection manipulation (augmentation, balancing, resampling) is described for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools are used in creating the MATH dataset; problems and solutions come from official competition sources.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of mathematics competition problems and solutions; no personal or sensitive information is collected.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: No explicit bias acknowledgements or bias-mitigation design decisions are discussed for the MATH dataset.
